opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. For me it wasn't one single moment; it built up over years of watching these systems do things we didn't think were possible.

When I started in deep learning, a lot of the work was on perception: getting networks to read text in natural images, recognize objects, that kind of thing. Even then you could see that if you set up the problem right, with the right data and the right objective, these models would find solutions that were better than anything we could hand-engineer. That was the first hint.

Then at DeepMind I worked on reinforcement learning and multi-agent systems, things like agents learning to play complex games together. What struck me there was that you could put learning systems into environments that were really rich and open-ended, and they would discover strategies and behaviors nobody had programmed in. They were creative in a way. That made me think the bottleneck wasn't really the learning algorithms anymore. It was whether we could point them at the right problems.

The real turning point was seeing AlphaFold. Protein structure prediction had been a grand challenge in biology for fifty years, with a well-defined benchmark and decades of very smart people working on it. Deep learning came in and essentially solved a large part of it. That was the proof point for me. It showed this wasn't just about games or benchmarks. These methods could crack fundamental scientific problems, and the impact on the real world could be enormous.

So once you see that, the question becomes: where else can we apply it? Drug discovery felt like the obvious next frontier. It's slow, expensive, and has high failure rates, yet it's ultimately about understanding and designing molecules and how they interact in biology. That's exactly the kind of complex, data-rich problem where learning systems can really shine. That's what pulled me toward working on it full time.

r001.rationale: The response describes deep learning succeeding in perception, games, and protein structure prediction, and suggests applying it to drug discovery. It does not clearly identify the transferability of deep learning’s fundamental building blocks across those domains.

r002.rationale: The response says confidence built over years of seeing systems do unexpected things and highlights AlphaFold’s success on a longstanding challenge. It does not attribute that confidence to repeatedly seeing teams solve problems leading researchers thought were still a decade away.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it wasn't one moment, it was more of a slow accumulation. When I started my PhD in Oxford, deep learning was still slightly fringe. People were doing hand-engineered features for computer vision, and the idea that you could learn everything end to end from data was treated with a bit of suspicion. But I was working on text recognition in natural images, reading text in the wild, and the moment we replaced the whole hand-crafted pipeline with a convolutional network trained on synthetic data, it just blew everything else away. That was the first time I personally felt it: this isn't an incremental technique, this is a different way of building systems.

Then at DeepMind the thing that really shifted my view was seeing the same underlying ideas work across completely different domains. We went from Atari to Go to StarCraft, and the common thread wasn't domain expertise, it was scalable learning. Every time we thought we'd hit a ceiling, it turned out that more data, more compute and a slightly better learning signal pushed through it. When you see that pattern repeat enough times, you stop thinking about whether deep learning works and start asking where the problems are whose structure matches that recipe.

And for me that question pointed very clearly at biology. Biology is the ultimate high-dimensional, data-rich, poorly understood system. Humans are not good at reasoning about it in the raw. AlphaFold was the proof point that these methods could do something scientists had been trying to do for fifty years. Once that landed, it felt obvious that the next decade was about applying this kind of learning to drug discovery, to understanding disease, to things that genuinely change people's lives rather than just winning games. That's what pulled me into what I'm doing now.

r001.rationale: The response says the same underlying ideas worked across Atari, Go, and StarCraft, identifying deep learning’s transfer across domains.

r002.rationale: It describes repeated progress across domains and pushing past ceilings, but does not say leading researchers thought these problems were still a decade away.

astra-6.text:
For me, it was seeing that the same basic approach—learning from data—could work across very different problems. You could move from recognizing what’s in an image to learning how to act, how to plan, how to solve a problem. That suggested we weren’t just building a better tool for one narrow task; we were developing something much more general.

And that changes the question you ask. Instead of, “Can we improve this benchmark?” you start asking, “Where could this capability make a real difference?” Scientific discovery is a particularly exciting example: if we can help explore possibilities that are too vast for people to work through directly, then we have a chance to change what we’re able to discover. That was the shift for me—from recognizing patterns to helping create new knowledge.

r001.rationale: The response says the same basic approach—learning from data—works across very different problems, including image recognition, acting, planning, and problem solving.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention teams solving problems that leading researchers thought were a decade away.

sol-6.1.text:
For me, it was seeing that the same basic approach could work across very different problems. You could train a neural network on images and get remarkable results, and then use those same underlying ideas to learn how to act—to make decisions, rather than just recognize things.

That suggested something much broader than a better solution to one particular task. If we could build systems that learn useful representations and discover strategies for themselves, we could start applying them to problems where we don’t already know how to write down the solution. That’s what made the potential feel transformative to me.

r001.rationale: The response says the same underlying approach works across very different problems, including image recognition and decision-making, communicating transferability across domains.
